questions.qtext:
A university schedules several exams on a single day.
Each exam is defined by a start time and an end time, and once an exam begins, it occupies one classroom continuously for its entire duration.
Two exams cannot be conducted in the same classroom if their time intervals overlap, including the case where one exam starts exactly at the same time another exam ends.
Given this scheduling constraint, determine the minimum number of classrooms required so that all exams can be conducted without any conflict.
Which of the following best describes this minimum number?

options.text: The total number of exams scheduled during the day
The maximum number of exams that overlap at any single point in time
The minimum number of exams that overlap at any single point in time
The number of distinct start times among all exams

questions.qtext:
Consider a system with a total of \(\mathbf{150}\) units of memory. Three processes are currently in the system, with their maximum memory needs and current allocations shown below:

\[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Process} & \textbf{Max Demand} & \textbf{Currently Holds} \\ \hline P1 & 70 & 45 \\ P2 & 60 & 40 \\ P3 & 60 & 15 \end{array} \]

A new process \(P4\) enters the system with a maximum memory requirement of \(60\) units.
Depending on its initial request, the state of the system may or may not remain safe.

Which of the following statements correctly describes the safety of the system?

options.text: If the system grants \(P4\)'s request of \(\;25\;\) units, the resulting state is unsafe because only \(\;25\;\) units remain and no process can finish.
If the system grants \(P4\)'s request of \(\;25\;\) units, the resulting state is safe because at least one of \(P1\) or \(P2\) can definitely complete.
If the system grants \(P4\)'s request of \(\;35\;\) units, the resulting state is safe because \(\;15\;\) units remain and \(P3\) can finish first.
If the system grants \(P4\)'s request of \(\;35\;\) units, the resulting state is safe only if \(P1\) finishes before \(P2\) and \(P3\).

questions.qtext:
Two processes compete for entering a critical section using a simple spin lock. Each process follows the pattern entry → critical section → exit exactly once. There is no while(1) or repetition of the critical section; each process tries to enter its critical section only one time.

It is possible that the system initially starts with only one of the processes in the ready state, while the other process becomes ready at some later time. (Both processes need not be ready at the start.)

// ENTRY SECTION
while (test_and_set(t));
// CRITICAL SECTION (executed once)
// EXIT SECTION
t = 0;

The instruction test_and_set(X) is atomic: it returns the old value of X and then sets X = 1.

Consider the following types of schedulers:

  • Priority scheduler: Higher-priority processes always run before lower-priority ones.
  • Round-robin scheduler: Preemptive, each process gets periodic CPU time.

Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding possible deadlock? (Multiple options may be correct.)

options.text: Under a priority scheduler, deadlock is possible.
Under a priority scheduler, deadlock cannot occur.
Under a round-robin scheduler, deadlock cannot occur.
Under a round-robin scheduler, deadlock is possible.

Given positive integers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k \).

For a positive integer \( x \) and \( j \le k \), let \( D(x, j) \) denote the number of ways to write \( x \) as the sum of numbers chosen from \( \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_j\} \), where each number can be used at most once and order does not matter.

For example, if \( a_1 = 1, a_2 = 2, a_3 = 3 \) and \( a_4 = 4 \), then there are exactly two ways to write \( x = 5 \) using \( \{a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4\} \), namely:

\( 5 = 2 + 3 = 1 + 4 \)

Hence, \( D(5,4) = 2 \).

 

For the purpose of this question, you do not need to worry about base cases.

Which of the following recurrence relations correctly computes \( D(x, j) \)?

questions.qtext:
If \(G\) is a context-free grammar with start symbol \(S\), then \(G'\), the augmented grammar for \(G\), is obtained by introducing a new start symbol \(S'\) and the production \(S' \rightarrow S\).

In the context of LR(0) parsers, an LR(0) item (item for short) of grammar \(G'\) is a production of \(G'\) with a dot at some position of the body.

We divide the LR(0) items of \(G'\) into two classes:

  1. Kernel items: The initial item \(S' \rightarrow \cdot S\), and all items whose dots are not at the left end.
  2. Nonkernel items: All items with their dots at the left end, except for \(S' \rightarrow \cdot S\).

Each state of the LR(0) automaton represents a set of items. Which of the following is/are true about the states in LR(0) automaton for grammar \(G'\):

options.text: Each state is the closure of a set of kernel items.
Each state is the closure of a set of nonkernel items.
If all nonkernel items are removed from a state, they can always be regenerated by applying the closure operation to the remaining items.
If any kernel item is removed from a state, it can never be regenerated by applying the closure operation to the remaining items.

Let transactions $\mathrm{T1}$, $\mathrm{T2}$, and $\mathrm{T3}$ be defined to perform the following operations:

  • $\mathrm{T1}:$ Add one to $A$
     
  • $\mathrm{T2}:$ Double $A$
     
  • $\mathrm{T3}:$ Display the current value of $A$ on the screen and then set $A$ to one

(where $A$ is some numeric item in the database).

Suppose the internal structure of $\mathrm{T1}$, $\mathrm{T2}$, and $\mathrm{T3}$ is as indicated below:
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\mathrm{T}_1 & \mathrm{T}_2 & \mathrm{T}_3 \\ \hline
\begin{array}{c}
\mathrm{F}_1:\ \text{fetch } A \text{ into } \mathrm{t}_1 \\
\mathrm{t}_1 := \mathrm{t}_1 + 1
\end{array}
&
\begin{array}{c}
\mathrm{F}_2:\ \text{fetch } A \text{ into } \mathrm{t}_2 \\
\mathrm{t}_2 := \mathrm{t}_2 * 2
\end{array}
&
\begin{array}{c}
\mathrm{F}_3:\ \text{fetch } A \text{ into } \mathrm{t}_3 \\
\text{display } \mathrm{t}_3
\end{array}
\\ \hline
\mathrm{U}_1:\ \text{update } A \text{ from } \mathrm{t}_1
&
\mathrm{U}_2:\ \text{update } A \text{ from } \mathrm{t}_2
&
\mathrm{U}_3:\ \text{update } A \text{ from } 1
\\ \hline
\end{array}
$$
Suppose transactions $\mathrm{T1}$, $\mathrm{T2}$, and $\mathrm{T3}$ are allowed to execute concurrently. If $A$ has initial value zero, how many possible values are displayed by $\mathrm{T3}$?

Let $M$ be a Turing machine over the alphabet $\Sigma$. We denote by $\operatorname{ACCEPT}(M)$ the set of strings accepted by $M$. A language $L \subseteq \Sigma^{*}$ is called Turing-recognizable if there exists a Turing machine $M$ such that $L=\operatorname{ACCEPT}(M)$. We use $\operatorname{TR}(L)$ to denote that the language $L$ is Turing-recognizable. In this sense, analyze the following statements about two languages $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ over the alphabet $\Sigma$ :

  1. If $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{1}\right)$ and $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{2}\right)$, then $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{1} \cup L_{2}\right)$.
     
  2. If $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{1}\right)$, then $\operatorname{TR}\left(\Sigma^{*} \backslash L_{1}\right)$.
     
  3. If $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{1}\right)$ and $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{2}\right)$, then $\operatorname{TR}\left(L_{1} \cap L_{2}\right)$.

According to the $\textsf{IEEE}$ standard, a $32$-bit, single-precision, floating-point number $\mathrm{N}$ is defined to be
$$
\text{N}=(-1)^\text{S} \times 1 . \text{F} \times 2^{\text{E}-127}
$$
where $\mathrm{S}$ is the sign bit, $\mathrm{F}$ the fractional mantissa, and $\mathrm{E}$ the biased exponent.

A floating-point number is stored as $\text{S : E : F},$ where $\text{S, E},$ and $\text{F}$ are stored in $1$ bit, $8$ bits, and $23$ bits, respectively.

What is the decimal value of the floating-point number $\textsf{C1E00000}$ (hexadecimal notation)?

questions.qtext:
An operating systems student is attempting reverse engineering of a machine whose page table was lost after a crash. Only a small log of recent address translations is available, and the student wants to reconstruct the missing page table entries from this behavior.

The available address translation log is shown below.

\[ \begin{array}{c c c} \text{Virtual address} & & \text{Physical address} \\ \hline \text{0x1063} & \rightarrow & \text{0x2063} \\ \text{0x584a} & \rightarrow & \text{0xe84a} \\ \text{0x4dfe} & \rightarrow & \text{Invalid} \\ \text{0x2a9f} & \rightarrow & \text{0x9a9f} \end{array} \]

The system configuration is as follows.

\[ \text{Virtual address space} = 32\text{ KB}, \quad \text{Physical memory} = 64\text{ KB}, \quad \text{Page size} = 4\text{ KB} \]

A simple linear page table is used, where each page table entry stores a valid bit and a physical frame number (PFN) and is written in the form $ (\text{Valid bit}, \text{PFN}) $. Let \(\text{PTE}\) denote the page table implemented as an array, where \(\text{PTE}[i]\) represents the entry corresponding to virtual page number \(i\).

Based only on the above log, select all options that must be correct.
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

questions.qtext:
A sender \(S\) communicates with a receiver \(D\) using a TCP variant where duplicate ACKs are ignored and loss detection occurs only via timeout. The retransmission timeout is \(\mathrm{RTO}=3\) RTTs. Transmission starts at \(t=0\) in slow start, packet numbering begins at \(1\), and the \(14^{\text{th}}\) packet is lost during its first transmission.

We assume continuous transmission at the sender: as soon as transmission of one window completes, transmission of the next window begins; i.e., the sender always has data to send.

The slow-start threshold is \(\mathrm{ssthresh}=18\) MSS.

Packets sent at the start of each RTT are partially shown below:

\[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{RTT start} & \text{Packets sent} \\ \hline 1 & 1 \\ \hline 2 & 2,\;3 \\ \hline 3 & \text{(Not given)} \\ \hline 4 & \text{(Not given; packet }14\text{ is lost)} \\ \hline 5 & ? \end{array} \]

Which of the following correctly represents the packets transmitted at the start of RTT \(5\)?

The routing tables configured on the three routers are shown below.

Router 1 \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Destination} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 128.100.11.32/27 & I2 \\ 128.100.11.0/24 & I3 \\ 0.0.0.0/0 & I1 \end{array} \]

Router 2 \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Destination} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 128.100.11.32/27 & I2 \\ 0.0.0.0/0 & I1 \end{array} \]

Router 3 \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Destination} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 128.100.11.16/28 & I2 \\ 128.100.11.0/24 & I3 \\ 0.0.0.0/0 & I1 \end{array} \]

Due to the above routing configuration, packets destined to some IP addresses enter a routing loop.

Which of the following destination IP addresses, when received at Router 1, will result in packets looping indefinitely in the network?

Consider the sliding window packet transmission scenario shown below.

  • Packet 2 is lost during transmission
  • At time t (indicated by the horizontal dashed line in the figure), the following ACKs are currently propagating from receiver to sender:
    • ACK0
    • ACK1
    • ACK3
  • No ACK has yet been received by the sender by time t

Answer the following based only on future events at the sender after time t.

Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If ACK0 is the next ACK received, the sender will advance its window and transmit packet 4.
If ACK1 is the next ACK received (and ACK0 is lost), the sender will advance its window to start at packet 2, but will not transmit any new packet.
If ACK2 is the next ACK received (and ACK0 and ACK1 are lost), the sender will advance its window and transmit packet 6.
If ACK3 is the next ACK received (and ACK0 and ACK1 are lost), the sender will mark packet 3 as acknowledged but will not advance the window.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following C program:

#include <stdio.h>
int mystery(int *p, int n)
{
 if (n <= 1)
 return *p;
 int y = mystery(p + 1, n - 1);
 return (*p > y) ? *p : y;
}
int main()
{
 int a[5] = {12, 7, 45, 23, 9};
 printf("%d", mystery(a, 5));
 return 0;
}

What will be the output of the program?
